findings.title: Dead `has_option` variable in verb_subform_is_read never read by any branch
findings.why_it_matters: A maintainer adding a new verb branch may reasonably assume has_option is live state to consult -- it is computed from a real per-token scan and threaded through the shared pre-loop before the case dispatch -- and spend time trying to use it or puzzling over why their new branch doesn't need it. It is write-only: computed at lines 131/141/145 and immediately discarded at line 235, so removing it changes no behavior, but its presence signals a distinction the code doesn't actually make. The comment justifying it ("so the body above stays readable if a future form needs it") is exactly the speculative-future-need reasoning that should not survive in committed code -- there is no current verb form that reads it.
evidence:
scripts/guard-shared-checkout:233-236: `# \`has_option\` n'est consulté par aucune branche ; il existe pour que le
    # corps ci-dessus reste lisible si une forme future en a besoin.
    : "$has_option"
    return 1`

None of the ten verb-specific case arms (branch, tag, stash, worktree, notes, submodule, remote, config, reflog, symbolic-ref) at lines 153-231 reference $has_option; each either re-scans args itself or checks $first_positional only.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete `local has_option=0` (line 131), the two `has_option=1` assignments (lines 141 and 145 -- simplify the bare `-*)` catch-all arm if it becomes a no-op), and the discard block (`: "$has_option"` plus its justifying comment, lines 233-235). If a future verb form genuinely needs an options-seen flag, add it scoped to that arm when it is written, rather than pre-declaring it here.

findings.title: 16 ad-hoc if/ok/ko content-assertion blocks duplicate a shape with no shared helper
findings.why_it_matters: The expect()/ok()/ko() trio cleanly covers every allow/deny-exit-code case (the majority of the 113+ cases), but assertions that check log-file content, stdout content, or the script's own source text -- bypass logging (258-262), deny-log content (271-275), fail-open-on-unwritable-log (283-294), the missing-script check (301-306), the hardcoded-path source scan (325-330), the hook-mode JSON/stdout checks (344-396), and the armor-line checks (410-421) -- each hand-roll their own `if [ ... ]; then ok "..."; else ko "..." "..."; fi` block instead of calling a shared assertion. A maintainer who wants to add one more "does the log contain X" case has no helper to call and must copy one of these ~16 blocks verbatim, which is exactly the kind of ad-hoc growth that drifts once one copy's condition is tightened or loosened and the others aren't updated to match.
evidence:
scripts/test-guard-shared-checkout.sh:258-262: `if [ -f "$BYPASS_LOG" ] && grep -q 'bypass' "$BYPASS_LOG"; then
	ok "la dérogation est journalisée (un contournement silencieux serait pire que pas de garde)"
else
	ko "la dérogation est journalisée" "aucune ligne « bypass » dans $BYPASS_LOG"
fi`

scripts/test-guard-shared-checkout.sh:271-275: `if [ -f "$DENY_LOG" ] && grep -q "deny project=$WT" "$DENY_LOG" && grep -q "target=$MAIN" "$DENY_LOG"; then
	ok "le refus journalise project-dir, cible et commande"
else
	ko "le refus journalise project-dir, cible et commande" "contenu: $(cat "$DENY_LOG" 2>/dev/null)"
fi` -- same if/grep/ok-else-ko shape repeated for a different log.
scripts/test-guard-shared-checkout.sh:283-294: two further instances of the identical shape for the fail-open-on-unwritable-log checks.
None of the ~16 content-checking blocks in this file call a shared helper analogous to expect(); each is written independently.
findings.suggested_fix: Extract one or two small helpers alongside expect()/ok()/ko() -- e.g. `assert_file_contains <file> <needle> <description>` and `assert_stdout_empty <description> -- <cmd...>` -- and route the ~16 hand-rolled content-check blocks through them. This is a test-file-only, non-behavioral change; expect() itself does not need to change since the allow/deny-exit-code cases it already covers are the majority and are well served as-is.

residual_risks: The four-term predicate (T1-T4), the fail-open rationale, and the arming-line mechanism are restated in prose across scripts/guard-shared-checkout's own header/decide_command doc-comment, CONTRIBUTING.md's new "Garde d'écriture git hors worktree" section, and .claude/settings.json's $comment. No structural link enforces agreement between these restatements -- a future change to any one term (e.g. adding a fifth predicate term, or changing which of the four measured occurrences this guard closes) can drift silently in the others, since only the behavioral test suite (test-guard-shared-checkout.sh) runs in CI, and it asserts the code's actual behavior, not that the prose describing it still matches.
testing_gaps: No test exercises the interaction between the PreToolUse hook's structured `deny` output and a permissions.allow entry covering Bash(git:*) -- the script's own header notes this precedence is unmeasured, which is why the guard signals refusal on two channels (stderr+exit-2 AND structured JSON) rather than relying on one. A test asserting which channel wins under Claude Code's current hook-precedence rules (or a comment recording that this is deliberately untested and why) would close this gap.
